VI. RELATIONSHIP BETWEEN LOCAL, SHORT-TERM USE OF MAN'S ENVIRONMENT AND THE MAINTENANCE AND ENHANCEMENT OF LONG-TERM PRODUCTIVITY
Fish and wildlife are a fundamental part of the natural environment and man's ecosystem. At one time man recognized that wildlife was essential to his survival because he depended upon it for food and clothing and other resources he needed for survival. A useful analogy is the dependence by Eskimos, until recently, upon wildlife for nearly all of life's needs. Over the centuries man was accustomed to a general over-abundance of fish and wildlife and gave little thought to the ultimate decimation of species. He was, of course, familiar with the consequences of a shortage of wildlife and learned to move his habitation to areas of suitable wildlife abundance.
As man developed technologies, he learned to substitute resources from agriculture, animal husbandry, and industrial processes to take the place of needs that had been supplied by wildlife. The importance of wildlife came to be recognized mainly as a luxury in man's environment. As man's hunger for the Earth's natural resources expanded and his technology developed to enable him to recover and refine those resources, he did so with little consideration for the effect on wildlife. As a result fish and wildlife populations diminished; entire species of animals disappeared with increasing frequency.
Thus we see the result of man's short-term use of his environment.

Little consideration was given to perpetuation of the resource. The only thought was today's needs with essentially no planning for tomorrow.
With the numbers of people that occupy the Earth today, there is much doubt that we could have all kinds of wildlife in the abundance our grand-fathers knew. But we could have fish and wildlife in far greater abundance
